title: MA7-03724
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Cuba and of Spain, is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant was persecuted in Cuba because of her membership in the family social group. Her son-in-law, her daughter's husband, is a political activist opposed to the Castro regime. Fleeing persecution, he was found to be a refugee in Canada in 2002; since then, the claimant, who stayed in Cuba, continues to be harassed, discriminated against, threatened and assaulted-she and her daughter were XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant's written narrative mentions several incidents of persecution. The claimant left Cuba in XXXXX 2007, to claim refugee protection in Canada.
The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity, which she established by the identity documents submitted on file.1

The claimant, a 79-year old woman, is suffering from an advanced stage of Alzheimer's disease and submitted evidence to that effect;2 she testified only briefly at her hearing, and a designated representative ensured her interests. Her son-in-law testified.

The panel finds the evidence concerning her fear of persecution in Cuba credible, and as the panel stated at the hearing, it is of the opinion that the claimant met her burden of proof concerning Cuba. The determinative issue is therefore whether the claimant established a well-founded fear of persecution or a fear under section 97 of the IRPA in Spain, her other country of citizenship? The panel is of the opinion that she did not, for the following reasons.

In her written narrative, the claimant does not indicate any fear of persecution or danger mentioned in section 97, in Spain. Her son-in-law, questioned at the hearing, testified that the claimant has no fear in Spain that would be related to her fear in Cuba.

In fact, what the claimant fears, as expressed by her son-in-law and by her designated representative, is the psychological and physical decompensation that she would experience upon a return to Spain, a country that she does not know, where she has never lived and where she has no family. In addition, her lawyer pleaded that she would not have a right to any social benefits because, according to the law, such benefits are conditional upon a stay in Spain of a minimum period of five years; he submitted evidence to corroborate that allegation.3 Upon a removal to Spain, she would be sentenced to begging, to a fast and marked deterioration of her health, and to an undoubted premature death, according to her son-in-law. Therefore, the claimant's lawyer pleaded that Spain does not offer effective protection for the claimant and that, therefore, she should be accepted as a refugee in Canada.

This argument cannot be used. The claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution in Cuba, but she has not established a fear of persecution in Spain. The fact that she could not receive social benefits because she has never lived in Spain does not constitute persecution but the application of a general law. In fact, it is not because of one of the grounds of the Convention that she would be refused social benefits-this law applies indiscriminately to everyone to whom it applies.

The claimant's lawyer argued that the denial of social benefits for the claimant is a refusal of protection indicated in sections 98 and 99 of the Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status: 98. Being unable to avail himself of such protection implies circumstances that are beyond the will of the person concerned. There may, for example, be a state of war, civil war or other grave disturbance, which prevents the country of nationality from extending protection or makes such protection ineffective. Protection by the country of nationality may also have been denied to the applicant. Such denial of protection may confirm or strengthen the applicant's fear of persecution, and may indeed be an element of persecution. 99. What constitutes a refusal of protection must be determined according to the circumstances of the case. If it appears that the applicant has been denied services (e.g., refusal of a national passport or extension of its validity, or denial of admittance to the home territory) normally accorded to his co-nationals, this may constitute a refusal of protection within the definition.
The claimant's lawyer pleaded that the claimant's illness is such that she cannot claim protection in Spain, so the sections mentioned above apply.

The panel does not agree with this interpretation. Although her illness is an independent circumstance of her will, the claimant is not unable to claim protection based on a situation of war in Spain, as the Handbook states. The panel notes that the claimant, herself, [translation] "cannot" claim protection from Spain; however, her family could easily appoint a legal representative who would ask for protection for her, as they did to produce a legal opinion. This situation is similar to that for minor children who will not themselves claim protection from authorities but for whom we expect the parents or representatives to ask for protection in their name.

Moreover, the panel is of the opinion that the protection identified in the IRPA is protection from persecution or the risks alleged under section 97; consequently, if the claimant has no fear of persecution and does not run any risk identified under section 97, her lawyer will be unable to claim that Spain will not protect her. The protection requested must be in connection with a fear mentioned in sections 96 or 97 of the IRPA.

I am very well aware that this situation places the claimant in a critical situation. Her lawyer alleges that the panel possesses the additional power of taking into account humanitarian and compassionate considerations; unfortunately for the claimant, the panel has no such power.

The lawyer alleges that the panel could assess the possibility of the claimant going to live in Spain, by applying the reasoning of the internal flight alternative. In fact, the notion of internal flight alternative, which is well-established in Canadian refugee law, foresees a component in which the reasonableness of the internal flight alternative must be assessed while taking into account all the circumstances, including the particular circumstances of the claimant.

This argument is clever but I cannot allow it; in fact, jurisprudence is constant in that claimants who are citizens of several countries must demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution or a risk, under section 97, in all of their countries of citizenship. This situation can seem unjust in that it implies a heavier burden of proof on a person who has more than one country of citizenship, while the reality of a person who has to relocate to a completely unknown country implies tribulations that are much greater than if they had to just change regions in their country. The panel is aware of this paradox; however, the panel must apply the law as it is today.

The refugee protection claim is rejected.
